skegness.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Skegness
s1loc: Skegness Foodbank runs from The Storehouse, an independent project kept going by volunteers and donations from local churches, businesses and individuals, handing out three-day emergency parcels on a referral basis. St Barnabas Hospice runs two charity shops in the town, on Lumley Road and Drummond Road, raising funds for palliative care across Lincolnshire. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, channel surplus stock to community groups along this stretch of coast, and the Greater Lincolnshire Food Partnership ties the local effort together.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities such as St Barnabas keep busy high-street shops with central buying and uniform standards, while small community groups, the one-room foodbank at The Storehouse, faith-run pantries and volunteer-led projects get by on a shoestring across Skegness, Winthorpe and the wider Lincolnshire coast. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Beyond the foodbank, the town leans on its volunteer base for everything from charity-shop tills to seasonal fundraising. St Barnabas has appealed publicly for more shop volunteers in Skegness to process donations and serve customers, and the How Are You Lincolnshire directory lists the local volunteering routes. Churches across the resort and out towards Ingoldmells host warm-welcome sessions and signposting, and the Lincolnshire Co-op food-bank collection points feed parcels to The Storehouse, knitting together a network that stretches inland to the market towns.

biddulph.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Biddulph
s1loc: Biddulph sits within the Stoke-on-Trent Foodbank network, which runs distribution points from churches including English Martyrs RC Church in the town and takes donations dropped at the Sainsbury's on Wharf Road. Dougie Mac, the Donna Louise hospice charity better known as Douglas Macmillan, runs a charity shop at 63 High Street that recruits local volunteers for sorting and till work. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, supply surplus food to community projects across the Staffordshire Moorlands.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep High Street shops with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the Biddulph Local People's Group, Methodist church projects and volunteer-run pantries operate on a shoestring across Biddulph, Knypersley and Brown Lees. Support Staffordshire in nearby Leek helps these tiny groups with funding and volunteers. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Biddulph Works Together coordinates a Warm Welcome offer across the town, drawing in the Methodist Church and Victoria Centre, the Biddulph Youth and Community Zone on Church Road and a string of community churches. Volunteers cover the Dougie Mac shop, the church-run foodbank sessions at St John's in Knypersley and seasonal collections, with the town directory and Biddulph Town Hall as the local hub. The effort reaches towards Congleton and Kidsgrove, where neighbouring foodbanks and shops share the same volunteer pool.

dorchester.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Dorchester
s1loc: Dorchester Foodbank runs from the Dorford Centre on Bridport Road, providing in-date basic food to people in crisis through vouchers issued by Citizens Advice, health visitors, social workers and church leaders. Weldmar Hospicecare, the county hospice charity, keeps shops and a furniture clearance outlet at Poundbury West Industrial Estate and the Marabout Trading Estate. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, now deliver to a growing chain of pop-up larders across Dorset, supporting frontline groups around the county town.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities such as Weldmar run busy shops with central buying and a clearance outlet, while small community groups, the Dorchester Community Church foodbank, CasterFridge the community fridge and volunteer larders get by on a shoestring across Dorchester, Poundbury and Fordington. Volunteer Centre Dorset ties it together. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Volunteer Centre Dorset, working with Dorset Council under the Dorset Community Response banner, recruits and places volunteers across the town and runs CasterFridge, the community fridge that rescues edible food for anyone regardless of means. Weldmar relies on shop volunteers to keep its Poundbury and Marabout outlets running, and the HelpAndKindness directory lists dozens of food-crisis and volunteering openings within ten miles of Dorchester. From the Dorford Centre out to Charminster, churches and community halls host the parcels, drop-ins and fundraising that keep the network alive.

atherton.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Atherton
s1loc: Atherton and Leigh Foodbank, a charity founded by local churches and community groups and partnered with the big national foodbank network, has helped people in crisis for over a decade. It runs four centres, one in Atherton, two in Leigh and one in Platt Bridge, each opening for a couple of hours on its given day to hand out three days of emergency food. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, channel surplus stock to community projects across this corner of the Wigan borough.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep shops with central buying along the town's parades, while small community groups, the Atherton and Leigh Foodbank's volunteer-run centres, church projects and mutual-aid efforts operate on a shoestring across Atherton, Hindley and Platt Bridge. The Wigan Borough Volunteering Hub places willing hands where they are needed. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

The foodbank leans heavily on supermarket collections, holding regular drives at stores in Atherton, Leigh and Hindley and filling around 150 two-hour slots across the Tesco Every Can Helps weekends at the Atherton and Leigh stores. Local churches and community groups supply the cash, food and volunteers that keep the four centres open, offering a warm welcome, a listening ear and signposting. The Wigan Borough Volunteering Hub and Reach Volunteering advertise the trustee, driver and warehouse roles that knit Atherton's effort into the wider Leigh and Wigan network.

failsworth.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Failsworth
s1loc: Failsworth falls within the Oldham Foodbank network, which works on a voucher referral system and relies on local food donations, volunteers and finances, taking stock at its base on Vulcan Street. Age UK Oldham runs a charity shop in the Failsworth Shopping Precinct, and the Hollins Food Pantry at Hollins Methodist Church serves the Limeside and Hollinwood area for a small donation. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, supply surplus food to projects across the borough.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities such as Age UK keep precinct shops with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the Hollins Food Pantry, church drop-ins and volunteer-led projects get by on a shoestring across Failsworth, Hollinwood and Medlock Vale. Action Together, the local infrastructure charity, backs these groups. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Action Together covers the Oldham South patch that takes in the Failsworth, Hollinwood and Medlock Vale wards, fielding a community development worker, running charity shops and keeping a directory of hundreds of weekly activities and social groups. Volunteers meet the Action Together team at Failsworth Library in the Town Hall, and the council's Failsworth and Hollinwood neighbourhood pages list the local wellbeing and food help. From the precinct out to Limeside, churches and community halls host the pantry sessions, parcels and fundraising that hold the network together.

colne.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Colne
s1loc: The Colne Open Door Centre on Great George Street runs as a not-for-profit community cafe, crisis drop-in and food-poverty resource open through the week, while St Bartholomew's Community Grocery serves shoppers from St Bartholomew's Church on Church Street every Monday. St John's Methodist Church hosts a foodbank in the town, and Pendleside Hospice keeps a charity shop on Dockray Street. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare, feed surplus stock to projects across Pendle and Burnley.

The sector here runs at every size. National charities such as Pendleside Hospice run a chain of shops with central buying, while small community groups, the Colne Open Door Centre, St Bartholomew's Community Grocery, the Madina Foodbank and volunteer pantries operate on a shoestring across Colne and Nelson. Spacious Place Engage coordinates much of the Pendle food provision. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Pendleside Hospice runs nine shops across Burnley and Pendle, including Colne, raising a substantial retail surplus and relying on volunteers across the chain, and has recently opened a tenth shop in Burnley. The Open Door Centre adds free counselling alongside its crisis cafe, and faith groups such as Nelson Community Mosque and Inspiring Grace run delivery foodbanks reaching Colne. From Church Street out to Waterside, churches, mosques and community halls host the parcels, food clubs and fundraising that link Colne into the wider Nelson and Burnley network.

bingley.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit across Bingley
s1loc: Bingley sits within the Feeding Bradford and Keighley network, a membership body of more than 90 organisations working against food poverty across the district, and is served by the wider Bradford foodbank provision. Sue Ryder runs a charity shop in the town centre, raising money for its Manorlands Hospice at nearby Oxenhope. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, including FareShare Yorkshire, redistribute surplus food to hundreds of charities and community groups across the county, reaching the Aire valley.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities such as Sue Ryder keep busy shops with central buying behind them, while small community groups, church-run foodbanks, holiday clubs and volunteer pantries get by on a shoestring across Bingley, Cottingley and Eldwick. Leeds Community Foundation has funded holiday clubs across the district. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts for the big names and direct online ordering with no minimum for the smallest group.

Sue Ryder Manorlands Hospice at Oxenhope provides palliative care across Airedale, Wharfedale, Craven and north Bradford, funded in part by its Bingley and Keighley shops and their volunteers. FareShare Yorkshire, founded in Barnsley, runs volunteer-driven warehouses that sort, store and assemble food orders for member charities, and the West Yorkshire Food Poverty Network ties the district together. From the town centre out to Gilstead and Crossflatts, churches and community halls host the food clubs, holiday provision and fundraising that connect Bingley into the Shipley and Keighley effort.
